Decision 
1. The appeals are dismissed. 
 
2. I found that the subject properties were hereditaments, and therefore dwellings, on the 
proposed effective date of 1 April 2025. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. The appeal process began when the appellant served proposals on the Listing Officer (LO) at 
the Valuation Office. The appellant made the proposals to have the subject properties deleted 
from the valuation list with effect from 1 April 2025. The LO issued her decisions in respect of 
the proposals on 29 September 2025, and these were challenged by way of appeals to the 
Valuation Tribunal on 28 December 2025. 
 
4. Within 24 hours of the hearing, one of the panel members advised they were no longer able to 
sit that day due to unforeseen circumstances. The Tribunal business arrangements provide 
that a Senior Member of the Tribunal may sit alone. I am therefore satisfied that I was 
authorised to hear and determine this appeal sitting alone.  
 
5. With the agreement of the parties, the panel varied the procedure outlined in the Consolidated 
Practice Statement PS8 – Model Procedure and invited the respondent to present her 
evidence first. 
 
6. This statement of reasons is not and does not purport to be a full verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Background 
 
7. The subject properties were three converted flats within one house. The properties were left to 
the appellant when his brother passed away. The properties had not been maintained for the 
previous 12 years prior to the appellant taking ownership. He was seeking deletion from 1 April 
2025 which is when he was able to provide photographic evidence from. He sought deletion 
on the basis the properties were derelict and beyond reasonable repair. 
 
8. The following case law was referred to at the hearing: 
 
• Wilson v Coll (Listing Officer) [2011] EWHC 2824 (Admin) 
• Newbigin (Valuation Officer) v S J & J Monk [2017] UKSC 14 
• Bunyan (Listing Officer) v Patel [2022] EWHC 1143 (Admin) 
Relevant Law 
 
The Local Government Finance Act 1992 
 
9. The legal basis of a dwelling for council tax purposes is that it must constitute a hereditament, 
in accordance with section 3 to the Local Government Finance Act 1992:   
 
“Meaning of “dwelling” 
3(1) This section has effect for determining what is a dwelling for the purposes of this Part. 

[2026] VTE VT00034454 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
3/5 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
 
3(2) Subject to the following provisions of this section, a dwelling is any property which – 
 
(a) by virtue of the definition of hereditament in section 115(1) of the General Rate Act 
1967, would have been a hereditament for the purposes of that Act if that Act 
remained in force; and 
 
(b) is not for the time being shown or required to be shown in a local or a central non-
domestic rating list in force at that time;” 
 
10. Section 115(1) of the General Rate Act 1967 defined a hereditament as: 
 
“property which is, or may be liable to a rate, being a unit of such property which is, or would 
fall to be shown as a separate item in the Valuation List.” 
 
11. A dwelling within the meaning of section 3, is a unit of property that qualifies as a hereditament 
because it is capable of beneficial occupation and is domestic property.  
 
Discussion 
 
12. The issue before me was to determine whether the properties should be deleted from the 
valuation list with effect from 1 April 2025, the date proposed by the appellant. Therefore, I 
must consider the physical state of the subject properties on that proposed effective date. 
 
13. The correct approach in appeals of this nature is to consider whether a hereditament exists at 
the proposed effective date. If it does, then it must be valued on the statutory assumption that 
it is in reasonable repair even if, in reality, it is in need of repair. 
 
14. In Wilson v Coll, the appeal property was generally in a poor condition, but capable of being 
repaired. In the judgement a distinction was drawn between the appeal property and one that 
was “truly derelict”. If a property was “truly derelict”, it would fail to be a hereditament and so 
not appear in the council tax list.  
 
15. In Newbigin v Monk, a non-domestic rating case, the Supreme Court decided that a property 
which was incapable of beneficial occupation due to a scheme of works was not a 
hereditament. In the subject appeal, there was no evidence of a scheme of works on the 
proposed effective date of 1 April 2025, or that any works had started at this point. The 
appellant stated at the hearing that works had not commenced, however they would be 
commencing imminently. 
 
16. In Bunyan v Patel, a council tax deletion appeal, the High Court considered whether the 
appeal property should be deleted from the valuation list. In that case, the landlord sought a 
deletion for poor repair the day after the tenant left the appeal property. The LO accepted that, 
about a year later, there was a scheme of works underway and those works were significant 
and would change the character of the property. The judge reviewed Wilson v Coll as well as 
Monk and concluded that the LO’s approach as set out in the Council Tax Manual was correct.  
 
17. I heard from Miss Portman that the external photographs provided showed that the overall 
structure appeared sound. She referred to a report from the local authority inspector who had 
visited the properties on 15 December 2025 which stated that there was no evidence the main 
structure was unsound.

18. Miss Portman stated that the list of works provided by the appellant was renovation works 
which had not begun. She did state that once the works began, the properties may qualify to 
be removed from the valuation list. This was not for me to consider at this hearing as it was an 
event which had not yet commenced. 
 
19. I heard from the appellant that it was his contention that the case law that had been referred to 
was nonsense and did not apply. He found it hard to fathom that there was no economic test 
to be considered. He argued that the cost to reinstate all three properties to a habitable 
condition would cost approximately £234,000. This was evidenced by the builder’s quote, 
however he stated this could increase if further works were discovered during the process. 
The appellant’s view was that the properties were beyond ‘reasonable repair’ at the proposed 
effective date and that the physical works required consisted of major replacement and 
reconstruction meant they were no longer dwellings. 
 
20. Through questioning I established that the hole in the roof the appellant had referred to was 
the plastic corrugated roof of the conservatory and that this was not built to the same standard 
as the main house. The appellant stated that there was no electrics, gas or water at the 
properties as the services had been turned off, however, he was unable to confirm if any pipes 
were removed or if there were services to the plot.  
 
21. I reviewed the photographs in the evidence bundle and the appellant assisted me by 
describing which flat each photograph was of. I accepted that the property was in poor repair. 
The appellant explained that vandals had been in the property and destroyed toilets and 
shattered the glass from some windows. The properties had been left with a significant amount 
of rubbish, holes had been made in some walls, and a significant amount of cleaning would be 
required. 
 
22. I acknowledged the appellant’s view of the case law; however, I am bound by the case law 
and the legislation in place when considering these appeals. No evidence had been provided 
to demonstrate that the properties were structurally unsound. I was of the view that the 
conservatory was not part of the main house when considering whether it was wind or 
watertight. The conservatory was made from inferior materials such as a corrugated plastic 
roof and was attached to the exterior brick wall of the house.  
 
23. I considered the case law before me and found that Monk v Newbigin did not apply in this 
case as there was no schedule of works currently taking place. The appellant confirmed at the 
hearing that there were currently no works taking place. Therefore, I had to consider whether, 
‘having regard to the character of the property and a reasonable amount of repair works being 
undertaken could the premises be occupied as a dwelling?’. This was identified as the correct 
test in Wilson v Coll and confirmed in Bunyan v Patel. 
 
24. The appellant stated that the subject property was uninhabitable. While I acknowledged that 
someone would not want to live in the subject property in its current state, when deciding this 
appeal, I was bound by the appropriate law which in this case is the Local Government 
Finance Act. The test is whether it was capable of repair and therefore remained a 
hereditament. 
 
25. Based on the evidence before me, both in the evidence bundle and the verbal evidence at the 
hearing, I am satisfied that the subject properties remained hereditaments and that the 
properties were not truly derelict. The evidence supported that the properties could be 
repaired. When considering reasonable repair, I am aware that Wilson v Coll established there 
was no economical test within the legislation for residential dwellings, however it would be

appropriate for me to consider the term reasonable. It is my view that the repair work required 
for the properties to be occupied as dwellings was reasonable. The cost of £234,000 listed in 
the quote provided by the builder was less than half of the value of the whole property in good 
condition, which the appellant had stated was £500,000 to £600,000. Therefore, I found that it 
would be reasonable for the repair work to be carried out on that basis. 
 
Conclusion 
 
26. In view of the above findings and conclusions, I was satisfied that the subject properties 
remained hereditaments, and therefore dwellings, on 1 April 2025, and therefore the appeals 
were dismissed. 
 
Right of further appeal 
 
27. Any party who is aggrieved at the Tribunal’s decision has a statutory right of further appeal to 
the High Court on a point of law pursuant to Regulation 43 of the Tribunal Procedure 
Regulations. A party does not require permission to appeal from the Tribunal. Any appeal 
must be made directly to the High Court using Form N161 (Appellant’s Notice) within four 
weeks of the date this decision and statement of reasons was issued. 
 
28. Further information regarding this statutory right of further appeal, and the parties’ other 
rights, is contained in the guidance booklet “A guide to tribunal decisions” available on the 
Tribunal’s website at www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk/guidance-booklets/.
